newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen presidential election race turns bitter.
newsitem.headline: Chechen presidential election race turns bitter.

text.p: The presidential election race in Russia's breakaway region of Chechnya is turning bitter as differences grow between leading candidates, despite pledges to keep a united front against Moscow.

Out of 16 candidates only five appear to have a realistic chance, including guerrilla commander Shamil Basayev, acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and Aslan Maskhadov, who recently resigned as head of the interim government.
Basayev on Thursday accused his rivals for the Chechen presidency in elections set for January 27 of turning their backs on the fighters who helped them drive out Russian forces.
He told a rally in the town of Argun near the capital Grozny that Russia was trying to foment discord among the separatists.
"Since the end of the war our leaders have pushed away the fighters who won our freedom...If this policy continues it could lead to a rift," said Basayev, dressed in combat fatigues.

Chechnya's polls campaign -- voters will also elect a parliament -- is now well under way across the tiny, oil-rich territory and the main candidates draw large crowds to their outdoor rallies despite freezing temperatures.
Basayev accused Yandarbiyev and Maskhadov of failing to tackle rising crime and wage and pension arrears.
But on Friday Maskhadov, who commanded Chechen forces during the war, pledged help for former fighters and their families.
"We will never forget the fallen and we will take good care of all those who survived," he told a rally at the village of Asinskaya, west of Grozny.
Maskhadov also distanced himself from the interim government and said Zavgayev and other "traitors" would all be punished.
Local people assailed the presidential candidates with complaints about lack of work and shortages of materials to rebuild their war-battered communities.

Maskhadov went out of his way to reassure Russians in the audience that their future would be secure in an independent Chechen state. "We are all the same under the law. Religion will not divide us, I want to assure you of this."
The election is part of a peace deal agreed with Moscow last August halting 21 months of fighting in which tens of thousands were killed and many more made homeless.

Campaign posters, mostly printed in Turkey and depicting the candidates' faces against the background of Chechnya's green, red and white flag, adorn cars and shop windows and most Chechens questioned by Reuters said they intended to vote.

Basayev, accompanied by gun-toting bodyguards, accused his rivals of surrounding themselves with supporters of Doku Zavgayev, the former pro-Moscow leader who is widely despised in the mountainous Caucasian region.
"This policy could lead to war among ourselves because our fighters could explode," he said, speaking in Chechen. "But we are all tired of fighting."
The bearded Basayev, who hijacked an aircraft to Turkey in 1991, became public enemy number one in Russia after leading a raid on the southern town of Budennovsk in June 1995.
A group of rebels under his command seized hostages in a hospital and more than 100 people were killed.
Basayev was speaking on the first anniversary this week of a raid led by another guerrilla leader, Salman Raduyev, in which dozens of people were killed in the neighbouring region of Dagestan.
At a separate rally in a cemetery where Chechen fighters killed in the raid are buried, Basayev said: "These graves show that our people have truly earned their independence."

Under last year's peace deal a decision on Chechnya's final political status was deferred for five years. Moscow hopes to persuade Chechnya to stay within the Russian Federation by providing economic incentives for the war-shattered region.
